title: Aesculapius
titleEn: The Serpent Comes to Rome — Metamorphoses XV.622–744
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: A deadly plague poisons the air of Latium, and when the physicians' arts fail the Romans go to Delphi. Apollo sends them on: they do not need Apollo but Apollo's son. Envoys sail to Epidaurus and ask the Greek council to give up their god; while the council argues, the god appears in a Roman's dream and promises to come in the form of the serpent that coils around his staff. At dawn a golden, high-crested snake glides from the temple, through the city, and aboard the Roman ship. The voyage up the coast becomes a catalogue of Italian headlands, harbours and towns. At the Tiber's mouth the whole population pours out to meet him; the ship is towed upstream between banks of smoking altars, and on the island in the river the god resumes his own shape, puts an end to the mourning, and comes to the city as a bringer of health.

sentences.t:
Pandite nunc, Musae, praesentia numina vatum
(scitis enim, nec vos fallit spatiosa vetustas,)
unde Coroniden circumflua Thybridis alti
insula Romuleae sacris adiecerit urbis.
sentences.l: Disclose now, Muses, you divinities present to poets — for you know, and the long stretch of antiquity does not escape you — how the island that deep Tiber flows around added the son of Coronis to the rites of Romulus's city.
sentences.i: Open it now, Muses, you powers ever present to poets — for you know, and the long reach of the past does not slip past you — how the island that deep Tiber flows around brought the son of Coronis into the rites of Romulus's city.
sentences.n: The episode opens with a fresh invocation, as if a new poem were beginning. “Coroniden” is a Greek patronymic accusative, “the son of Coronis” — that is, Aesculapius, the healing god. Worth noticing at the start: the printed heading names Aesculapius, but the name never appears in the Latin of this whole part. He is only ever “the son of Coronis”, “the Phoebean youth”, “the helping god”, “the Epidaurian”, “the Phoebean serpent”. “Adiecerit” is perfect subjunctive in an indirect question after “unde”. “Circumflua … insula” is the Tiber Island, and both words come back at the close (739 “circumfluus amnis”, 740 “Insula nomen habet”).

sentences.t:
Dira lues quondam Latias vitiaverat auras,
pallidaque exsangui squalebant corpora morbo.
sentences.l: A dreadful plague had once tainted the air of Latium, and pale bodies were foul with a bloodless disease.
sentences.i: A dreadful plague had once poisoned the air of Latium, and pale bodies lay squalid with a sickness that left them bloodless.
sentences.n: “Squalere” is to be rough, filthy, unkempt — the word for a neglected body or a mourner's unwashed clothes, not simply for illness. “Exsangui … morbo” is ablative of description or cause; the disease is called “bloodless” for what it does to the people who have it, an epithet transferred from sufferer to sickness. The pluperfect “vitiaverat” puts the plague already at work before the narrative proper starts.

sentences.t:
Funeribus fessi postquam mortalia cernunt
temptamenta nihil, nihil artes posse medentum,
sentences.l: After, worn out by funerals, they see that mortal attempts can do nothing, nothing the arts of the healers,
sentences.i: When, worn out with burials, they saw that human remedies could do nothing, and nothing the physicians' arts,
sentences.n: “Postquam … cernunt”: a present indicative after “postquam” where English wants a past — the historic present, which runs against perfects and pluperfects throughout this part and is worth watching, because the alternation is how Ovid speeds and slows the telling. “Nihil … posse” is accusative-and-infinitive with “nihil” as internal accusative, “can do nothing”, and the repetition (“nihil, nihil”) is the exhaustion of the line. “Medentum” is the genitive plural of the present participle of “medeor”, poetic for “medentium”: “of those who heal”, i.e. the doctors.

sentences.t:
auxilium caeleste petunt mediamque tenentes
orbis humum Delphos adeunt, oracula Phoebi,
sentences.l: they seek heavenly help, and they go to Delphi, holding the middle ground of the world, the oracles of Phoebus,
sentences.i: they sought help from heaven, and went to Delphi, which holds the earth's midpoint, the oracle of Phoebus,
sentences.n: “Delphos” is accusative plural — the place-name is plural in Latin — and “tenentes” is the participle agreeing with it. Delphi was held to be the navel of the world, the point where two eagles released by Jupiter from opposite ends of the earth met. “Oracula Phoebi” stands in apposition to “Delphos”: the place named by what it is for.

sentences.t:
utque salutifera miseris succurrere rebus
sorte velit tantaeque urbis mala finiat, orant:
sentences.l: and they pray that with a health-bringing response he be willing to come to the help of their wretched affairs and end the evils of so great a city:
sentences.i: and they pray that he will consent to relieve their misery with a saving oracle and put an end to so great a city's sufferings:
sentences.n: “Orant” with “ut … velit … finiat” is an indirect command, the two subjunctives carrying the substance of the prayer. “Sorte” is a “lot”: the oracle answered by lots, and the word came to mean the response itself. “Salutifera”, “health-bringing”, is the first appearance of the word the whole episode turns on — it returns as the last word but one of the part, at 744, “salutifer urbi”.

sentences.t:
et locus et laurus et, quas habet ipse, pharetras
intremuere simul, cortinaque reddidit imo
hanc adyto vocem pavefactaque pectora movit:
sentences.l: and the place and the laurel and the quivers which he himself holds trembled all together, and the cauldron gave back this voice from the innermost shrine and shook their fear-struck hearts:
sentences.i: the place, the laurel, and the quivers the god himself carries shuddered all at once; and from the depth of the sanctuary the cauldron gave back this voice and shook their terrified hearts:
sentences.n: “Intremuere” (opening line 635) is “intremuerunt”: the poetic third-plural perfect in -ēre, which you will meet constantly. It occurs seven times in this part — intremuere (635), accepere (641), tetigere (644), adiere (645), oravere (646), pepulere (651), advertere (719) — and after this note it will only get a nudge. The “cortina” is the great bowl of the Delphic tripod, from which the response came. One textual point: “intremuere” needs a nominative subject, and Magnus prints “pharetras”, accusative — the antecedent pulled into the case of its own relative “quas”, the figure called inverse attraction. The edition is followed exactly, and the word is read here as the third subject, which is what the sense requires; other editions print the regular nominative “pharetrae”.

sentences.t:
“Quod petis hinc, propiore loco, Romane, petisses,
et pete nunc propiore loco!
sentences.l: “What you seek from here, Roman, you could have sought in a nearer place — and seek it now in a nearer place!
sentences.i: “What you seek from here you might have sought nearer home, Roman — so seek it nearer home now!
sentences.n: “Petisses” is the syncopated form of “petivisses”, pluperfect subjunctive, used of what could have been done and was not. The oracle is a riddle: the “nearer place” turns out to be Epidaurus in the Argolid (643) — not in fact a shorter voyage than Delphi, so what is nearer is the god and not the sea-mileage. The singular vocative “Romane” addresses the whole Roman people as one man, and the god switches to the plural “vobis” in the very next line.

sentences.t:
nec Apolline vobis,
qui minuat luctus, opus est, sed Apolline nato.
sentences.l: and you have no need of Apollo, who would lessen your griefs, but of one born of Apollo.
sentences.i: and it is not Apollo you need to lessen your grief, but Apollo's son.
sentences.n: “Opus est” takes the ablative of the thing needed (“Apolline”) and the dative of the person needing it (“vobis”). “Qui minuat” is a relative clause of characteristic or purpose, hence the subjunctive: the sort of god who would reduce their mourning. “Apolline nato” is “born of Apollo”: “nato” is the participle used as a noun, the one born, and “Apolline” is ablative of origin with it. So the name Apollo stands twice in one sentence and names the father both times — the second time only as the parent of the god actually wanted.

sentences.t: Ite bonis avibus prolemque accersite nostram!”
sentences.l: Go with good birds, and fetch our offspring!”
sentences.i: Go under good omens, and fetch our son!”
sentences.n: “Bonis avibus”, literally “with good birds”, is the ordinary Roman idiom drawn from augury: under favourable auspices, with the omens right. “Accersite” is a common spelling of “arcessite”, “summon, send for”. Apollo speaks of himself in the plural (“nostram”), and “proles” is the formal word for offspring — the god names his son by relation rather than by name, as the poem does throughout.

sentences.t:
Iussa dei prudens postquam accepere senatus,
quam colat, explorant, iuvenis Phoebeius urbem,
quique petant ventis Epidauria litora mittunt.
sentences.l: After the far-seeing senate received the god's commands, they investigate which city the Phoebean youth inhabits, and they send men who are to make for the Epidaurian shores with the winds.
sentences.i: When the prudent senate had received the god's commands, they searched out which city the son of Phoebus dwelt in, and sent men to make for the shores of Epidaurus under sail.
sentences.n: “Prudens … senatus” is singular, but all three verbs — “accepere”, “explorant”, “mittunt” — are plural: agreement by sense rather than by form, since a senate is many men. (“Accepere” is another -ēre perfect.) “Quam colat … urbem” is an indirect question with the noun pulled inside it. “Quique petant” is “qui petant”, a relative clause of purpose after “mittunt”: men sent in order to seek. “Colere” of a place means to live in it and keep its rites, both at once.

sentences.t:
Quae simul incurva missi tetigere carina,
concilium Graiosque patres adiere,
sentences.l: As soon as the men sent touched these with a curving keel, they approached the council and the Greek fathers,
sentences.i: The moment the envoys touched those shores in their curving ship, they went before the council and the elders of Greece,
sentences.n: The sentence opens with a relative pronoun, “Quae”, whose antecedent is in the sentence before: the connecting relative, and it means “and these (shores)”, not “which”. Latin links sentences this way constantly, and English has to break the link into “and them”. “Carina” is the keel, standing for the whole ship — it does the same work again at 694 and 719. “Tetigere” and “adiere” are -ēre perfects.

sentences.t:
darentque,
oravere, deum, qui praesens funera gentis
finiat Ausoniae: certas ita dicere sortes.
sentences.l: and they begged that they should give up the god, who by being present might end the deaths of the Ausonian race: that unerring lots said so.
sentences.i: and begged them to give up the god, who by his presence might end the dying of the Ausonian people: unerring lots, they said, had spoken it so.
sentences.n: The verb of asking is postponed inside its own clause — “darentque, oravere, deum” — an interlacing Ovid likes, where the main verb is buried in the middle of what it governs. “Darent” is imperfect subjunctive in indirect command. “Praesens” of a god is a technical word: not merely present but present and effective, the god who actually shows up and acts. “Ausoniae” is Italian; Ausonia is an old poetic name for Italy, and it returns at 693. The closing “certas ita dicere sortes” is accusative-and-infinitive, the envoys' report continuing in reported speech; “certas” is an adjective with “sortes” — lots that are sure — not an adverb on the verb.

sentences.t:
Dissidet et variat sententia, parsque negandum
non putat auxilium, multi retinere suamque
non emittere opem nec numina tradere suadent:
sentences.l: Opinion is divided and shifts, and one part thinks the help must not be refused; many urge that they keep back and not send away their own aid, and not hand over their divinity:
sentences.i: Opinion divided and shifted: some thought the help should not be refused, while many urged holding back, not sending away the help that is theirs, not handing over their god:
sentences.n: “Negandum non putat auxilium” is a gerundive of obligation inside indirect statement: they think the help “is not to be refused”. “Pars” (singular) is balanced against “multi” (plural), the two halves of a divided house. “Opem” is help, resource, protection — the god considered as what he does for them. “Numina”, plural, is used of the single god here and again at 675; poetry treats the word almost as a collective. (At 622 the same plural was genuinely plural, of the Muses.)

sentences.t:
dum dubitant, seram pepulere crepuscula lucem,
umbraque telluris tenebras induxerat orbi,
sentences.l: while they hesitate, the twilight drove away the late daylight, and the shadow of the earth had drawn darkness over the world,
sentences.i: while they hesitated, dusk drove off the lingering light, and the earth's shadow had drawn darkness over the world,
sentences.n: “Dum” with a present indicative for past time (“while they were hesitating”) is the regular Latin idiom, and here the present sits between a perfect (“pepulere”, another -ēre form) and a pluperfect (“induxerat”) — three tenses in two lines, the narrative slowing as night comes on. “Umbra telluris” is not merely poetic: it is the earth's cone of shadow, the astronomical explanation of night, dropped in as a plain fact.

sentences.t:
cum deus in somnis opifer consistere visus
ante tuum, Romane, torum, sed qualis in aede
esse solet,
sentences.l: when the helping god seemed in sleep to stand before your bed, Roman — but such as he is accustomed to be in his temple,
sentences.i: when the healing god seemed in a dream to be standing before your bed, Roman — but looking as he does in his temple,
sentences.n: An inverted “cum” clause: grammatically subordinate, but it carries the real event of the sentence, while the main clause held only the falling of night. “Visus” stands for “visus est” — the copula is regularly left out with participles. “Opifer”, “help-bringing”, is a cult title of Aesculapius, not an ordinary adjective. And here Ovid turns aside to speak to his reader directly — “ante tuum, Romane, torum”, before your bed — the poem's own apostrophe, distinct from the god's vocative at 637; he does it again to Vesta at 730–731.

sentences.t:
baculumque tenens agreste sinistra
caesariem longae dextra deducere barbae
et placido tales emittere pectore voces:
sentences.l: and holding a rustic staff in his left hand, and drawing his right down the hair of his long beard, and sending out from a calm breast words such as these:
sentences.i: holding his countryman's staff in his left hand, drawing his right down the hair of his long beard, and uttering from a calm breast words like these:
sentences.n: “Sinistra” and “dextra” are ablatives with “manu” left out, the usual shorthand for “with the left / right hand”. The participle “tenens” and the two infinitives “deducere” and “emittere” all hang from “visus (est)” back at 653: he seemed to be stroking his beard and speaking. “Caesaries” properly means the hair of the head, used here of the beard. The staff is “agreste”, a plain countryman's stick — and it is the staff the serpent will be found coiled around at 659, four lines on.

sentences.t: “Pone metus! Veniam simulacraque nostra relinquam.
sentences.l: “Lay aside your fears! I shall come, and I shall leave my images behind.
sentences.i: “Put your fears aside! I shall come, and I shall leave my images behind me.
sentences.n: “Veniam” here is the future indicative of “venio”, “I shall come” — not the noun “venia”, pardon, which is spelled the same in the accusative. Context decides it, and the context is a promise. “Metus” is plural for the abstract, common in verse. “Simulacra nostra” are his cult statues at Epidaurus: the god leaves, the images stay — an answer in advance to the Greeks who did not want to give him up.

sentences.t:
Hunc modo serpentem, baculum qui nexibus ambit,
perspice et usque nota visu, ut cognoscere possis!
sentences.l: Only look closely at this serpent, which encircles my staff with its coils, and mark it thoroughly with your eye, so that you can recognize it!
sentences.i: Only look closely at this serpent that winds around my staff in its coils, and fix it well with your eyes, so that you will know it again!
sentences.n: “Modo” here is the adverb “only, just”, not a case-form of “modus”. “Nexibus” is ablative of means: with its knots, its interlacings. The imperatives “perspice” and “nota” are followed by a purpose clause, “ut … possis”. The serpent twined about the staff is the god's standing attribute in art and cult — and the point of the instruction is that the attribute is about to become the god himself.

sentences.t:
Vertar in hunc, sed maior ero tantusque videbor,
in quantum verti caelestia corpora debent.”
sentences.l: I shall be turned into this, but I shall be greater, and I shall appear as great as heavenly bodies ought to be turned into.”
sentences.i: Into this I shall be changed — but larger, and I shall look as large as heavenly bodies ought to become when they change.”
sentences.n: “Vertar” is passive in form, “I shall be turned”, but works as a middle: “I shall change myself”. Latin has no separate middle voice and uses the passive for it constantly, which is why so many transformations in this poem are grammatically things done to the person changing. “Tantus … in quantum” are correlatives, “so great … as great as”. The god announces his own metamorphosis before it happens, so the reader watches for the change rather than being surprised by it; he undoes it at 743.

sentences.t:
Extemplo cum voce deus, cum voce deoque
somnus abit, somnique fugam lux alma secuta est.
sentences.l: At once the god departs with the voice, and sleep with the voice and the god, and nourishing light followed the flight of sleep.
sentences.i: At once the god went with his voice, and sleep with the voice and the god; and kindly daylight followed sleep's retreat.
sentences.n: “Cum voce deus, cum voce deoque somnus” — the phrase repeats and grows, each departure taking the last one with it, and a single verb “abit” serves both subjects (agreeing with the nearer). “Alma” is the standing epithet of light and of nourishing things generally, from “alo”, to feed. “Secuta est” is the perfect of the deponent “sequor”: passive in form, active in meaning.

sentences.t: Postera sidereos aurora fugaverat ignes:
sentences.l: The next dawn had put the starry fires to flight:
sentences.i: The next dawn had routed the fires of the stars.
sentences.n: “Sidereos ignes” is the stars — fire is the poem's regular word for them. The pluperfect “fugaverat” places the whole of daybreak before the sentence that follows even begins: the day is already up, and the nobles are already uncertain. “Postera” is feminine nominative agreeing with “aurora” itself — the next day's dawn, not an adjective waiting on an understood “dies”.

sentences.t:
incerti, quid agant, proceres ad templa petiti
perveniunt operosa dei, quaque ipse morari
sede velit, signis caelestibus indicet, orant.
sentences.l: the chiefs, uncertain what they should do, come to the elaborate temples of the god who has been asked for, and they pray that he indicate by heavenly signs in what seat he himself wishes to stay.
sentences.i: The nobles, uncertain what to do, came to the richly worked temples of the god they had asked for, and prayed him to show by signs from heaven where he wished to settle.
sentences.n: “Incerti quid agant” is an indirect question with a deliberative subjunctive: “what are we to do?” put into the third person. “Petiti dei” is a genitive: the god they had requested from the Greeks — the participle keeps the sense of the envoys' asking at 645–647. “Operosa” of a building means worked over, elaborate, made with labour. A second indirect question (“qua … sede velit”) sits inside an indirect command (“indicet”) after “orant”. Magnus prints “perveniunt”, “they arrive at”; some editions print “conveniunt”, “they gather at”.

sentences.t:
Vix bene desierant, cum cristis aureus altis
in serpente deus praenuntia sibila misit
sentences.l: Scarcely well had they finished, when the god, golden with high crests, in a serpent sent out heralding hisses
sentences.i: They had scarcely properly finished when the god, golden and high-crested, in serpent form sent out a hiss of warning
sentences.n: Another inverted “cum” clause, and “vix bene” strengthens it: hardly, and not even properly. “Cristis … altis” is ablative of description — a crest is the mark of a sacred or portentous serpent, not of an ordinary snake, and Ovid gives it first, before the word “serpente” arrives. “In serpente deus” is exact: the god inside the serpent, not turned into one and gone. “Praenuntia” is a neuter plural adjective agreeing with “sibila”: hisses that announce beforehand.

sentences.t:
adventuque suo signumque arasque foresque
marmoreumque solum fastigiaque aurea movit
sentences.l: and by his coming he moved the statue and the altars and the doors and the marble floor and the golden gables
sentences.i: and by his coming shook the statue and the altars and the doors and the marble floor and the golden pediment
sentences.n: Five objects in two lines, each strung on its own “-que” — signum, aras, fores, solum, fastigia. The piling up (polysyndeton) makes the shaking travel from one thing to the next instead of happening all at once. “Signum” here is the cult statue; “fastigia” the gable of the temple front, gilded as the great temples were.

sentences.t:
pectoribusque tenus media sublimis in aede
constitit atque oculos circumtulit igne micantes.
sentences.l: and as far as his breast he stood high in the middle of the shrine and carried his eyes around, flashing with fire.
sentences.i: and reared breast-high in the middle of the shrine, and swept his fire-flashing eyes around him.
sentences.n: “Tenus” is a postposition: it governs the ablative and stands after its noun, so “pectoribus tenus” is “as far as the breast”. The plural “pectoribus” for a single chest is poetic licence. “Circumtulit” is literally “carried around”, of the sweep of a look. “Igne micantes” — a participle with the ablative of what it shines with.

sentences.t:
Territa turba pavet. Cognovit numina castos
evinctus vitta crines albente sacerdos:
sentences.l: The terrified crowd is afraid. The priest, bound as to his consecrated hair with a white band, recognized the divinity:
sentences.i: The crowd is terrified and cowers. The priest, his consecrated hair bound with a white fillet, knew the god:
sentences.n: “Evinctus … castos … crines” is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle: “bound as to his hair”, i.e. with his hair bound. The participle is passive in form but the priest did it to himself — Latin uses this to describe how someone is dressed or adorned. The construction runs through the whole poem, though this is its only occurrence in this part. The “vitta” is the white woollen fillet worn by priests, which is what identifies him. “Territa turba pavet” says the same thing twice over, and the alliteration on t drives the fright home.

sentences.t:
“En deus est deus est! Animis linguisque favete,
quisquis ades!” dixit.
sentences.l: “Behold, it is a god, it is a god! Be favourable with your minds and your tongues, whoever is present!” he said.
sentences.i: “Look — a god, a god! Keep your minds and your tongues holy, whoever you are that stand here!” he said.
sentences.n: The doubled cry is the formula of recognition at an epiphany — the god is not argued for but pointed at. “Animis linguisque favete” is Roman ritual language: “favete linguis” is the standing call for the reverent hush in which a rite must be performed, literally “be favourable with your tongues”, in practice “say nothing, and certainly nothing ill-omened”. “Quisquis ades” is singular — “whoever you are that are present” — spoken to each person in the crowd separately, and it is picked up at 680, “Quisquis adest … venerantur”, where the singular subject takes a plural verb.

sentences.t:
“Sis, o pulcherrime, visus
utiliter populosque iuves tua sacra colentes !”
sentences.l: “May you, most beautiful one, have been seen to good purpose, and may you help the peoples that tend your rites!”
sentences.i: “May the sight of you, most beautiful one, have been to our good, and may you aid the peoples who keep your rites!”
sentences.n: “Sis … visus” is a perfect passive subjunctive of “videor” used as a wish (optative subjunctive): may your having appeared turn out usefully for us. It is not a request that he be seen — he has been seen already — but a prayer about what the sight will mean. “Iuves” is a second wish alongside it. “Colentes” agrees with “populos”: the peoples who tend the rites, the same verb “colere” used of the city he lived in at 642. The edition prints a space before the exclamation mark at the end of this line (“colentes !”); it is set here exactly as printed.

sentences.t:
Quisquis adest, visum venerantur numen, et omnes
verba sacerdotis referunt geminata piumque
Aeneadae praestant et mente et voce favorem.
sentences.l: Whoever is present, they worship the divinity that has been seen, and all repeat the priest's words doubled, and the sons of Aeneas offer dutiful favour both with mind and with voice.
sentences.i: Every man there worships the god they have seen; all repeat the priest's words twice over, and the sons of Aeneas render their dutiful goodwill in mind and in voice alike.
sentences.n: “Quisquis adest … venerantur”: a singular subject with a plural verb, taken by sense — “whoever is there” means “all who are there”, the same construction as “senatus … explorant” at 641–642. “Geminata” agrees with “verba”: the crowd doubles the priest's cry, which was itself already doubled. “Favorem … praestant” answers his “favete” at 677 — the ritual goodwill he demanded is now given. “Aeneadae”, the sons of Aeneas, is a standing name for the Romans. Magnus prints “visum venerantur”, “they worship the god who has been seen”; some editions print “iussum veneratur”, which makes the object the god's command instead.

sentences.t:
Adnuit his motisque deus rata pignora cristis
et repetita dedit vibrata sibila lingua.
sentences.l: The god nodded assent to these things and, with his crests moved, gave sure pledges, and repeated hisses with his darting tongue.
sentences.i: The god assented, and with a stir of his crests gave sure pledges, and hissed again with a flickering tongue.
sentences.n: “Adnuit” is the nod — the standing sign of a god granting a prayer, and the root of the Latin word for a divine will. “Motis … cristis” is an ablative absolute: a self-contained phrase, “with his crests moved”, where English wants a clause or a gerund, “by moving his crests”. This construction runs through the rest of the part (“caeso … tauro”, 695; “Aequore placato”, 723; “specie … resumpta”, 743). “Rata pignora”: “ratus”, from “reor”, is what has been reckoned valid and fixed — pledges that will hold. Magnus prints “et repetita”; some editions print “ter repetita”, hissed three times, three being the ritual number.

sentences.t:
Tum gradibus nitidis delabitur oraque retro
flectit et antiquas abiturus respicit aras
adsuetasque domos habitataque templa salutat.
sentences.l: Then he glides down the gleaming steps and bends his face back and, about to depart, looks back at his ancient altars and salutes his accustomed home and the temples that have been lived in.
sentences.i: Then he slid down the polished steps, turned his head back, and, on the point of leaving, looked once more at his ancient altars and took his leave of the house he was used to and the temples he had lived in.
sentences.n: “Abiturus” is a future participle used of intention: about to go, meaning to go. “Salutat” is the word for a formal greeting and equally for a formal farewell — the departing householder's word, and it lands here on buildings rather than people. “Habitata templa” turns the passive participle onto the place: temples that have been lived in. Three verbs of looking and leaving in three lines, and the god does all of them while sliding away.

sentences.t:
Inde per iniectis adopertam floribus ingens
serpit humum flectitque sinus mediamque per urbem
tendit ad incurvo munitos aggere portus.
sentences.l: Then, huge, he creeps over ground covered with flowers thrown down on it, and bends his coils, and through the middle of the city makes for the harbour fortified with a curving mole.
sentences.i: Then, huge, he glided over ground strewn deep with flowers, winding his coils, and made through the middle of the city for the harbour walled by its curving mole.
sentences.n: “Per … adopertam … humum”: the preposition is torn away from its noun by everything that lies between (hyperbaton), and the flowers sit in the middle of the phrase as they sit on the ground. “Iniectis floribus” is ablative with “adopertam”, covered by flowers thrown on — the crowd strews his path as he goes. “Serpit” is the verb from which “serpens” is formed: the god does what a serpent is named for. “Aggere” is the built-up mole or breakwater of a harbour.

sentences.t:
Restitit hic agmenque suum turbaeque sequentis
officium placido visus dimittere vultu
corpus in Ausonia posuit rate:
sentences.l: Here he halted and, seeming with calm face to dismiss his own train and the attendance of the following crowd, laid his body in the Ausonian ship:
sentences.i: Here he halted and, with a calm look that seemed to release his escort and the attendance of the crowd behind him, laid his body in the Italian ship:
sentences.n: “Visus … dimittere”, “seemed to dismiss”, is the same construction as “consistere visus” at 653: the god's intention is read off his face, not spoken. “Officium” is the formal duty owed by an escort — what Romans performed for a departing magistrate or a friend leaving the city — so the crowd is being thanked and released, not driven off. “Ausonia … rate”: Ausonian for Italian again, as at 647.

sentences.t:
numinis illa
sensit onus, pressa estque dei gravitate carina;
sentences.l: she felt the weight of the divinity, and the keel was pressed down by the god's heaviness;
sentences.i: she felt the god's weight, and the hull was pressed down under his weight.
sentences.n: “Illa” picks up “rate” from the clause just before it in the same line, 693 — ships are feminine in Latin, and the pronoun is enough to carry her over the line-break. “Gravitas” is both physical weight and gravity in the moral sense, the seriousness and authority of the god; the ship registers his presence in the only way a ship can. “Carina”, the keel, stands for the whole ship, as at 644 and again at 719.

sentences.t:
Aeneadae gaudent caesoque in litore tauro
torta coronatae solvunt retinacula navis.
sentences.l: The sons of Aeneas rejoice and, with a bull slaughtered on the shore, loose the twisted cables of the garlanded ship.
sentences.i: The sons of Aeneas rejoiced, and with a bull killed on the shore they cast off the twisted hawsers of the garlanded ship.
sentences.n: “Caeso … tauro” is another ablative absolute, and it names the sacrifice made before a voyage. “Coronatae … navis”: a ship was garlanded for a festal or sacred sailing, and this one is carrying a god. “Torta retinacula” are the mooring ropes, “twisted” because rope is what twisting makes.

sentences.t:
Impulerat levis aura ratem: deus eminet alte,
impositaque premens puppim cervice recurvam
caeruleas despectat aquas
sentences.l: A light breeze had driven the ship forward: the god stands out high, and pressing the curved stern with his neck laid upon it he looks down on the dark-blue waters
sentences.i: A light breeze had pushed the ship on; the god towers high, and, laying his neck along the curving stern and pressing it down, looks down on the dark-blue water
sentences.n: A pluperfect (“Impulerat”) and then two presents (“eminet”, “despectat”): the breeze is already past, and the picture of the god riding the stern is held still in the present. “Imposita … cervice” is an ablative with a participle, the instrument of “premens” — with his neck laid along it — and “premens” makes the weight felt again, as the keel felt it at 694. “Puppim recurvam” is the high curved stern of an ancient ship, the natural place for a serpent to rest a head. “Caeruleus” is the sea's own colour word, a dark blue-green rather than sky-blue.

sentences.t:
modicisque per aequor
Ionium zephyris sextae Pallantidos ortu
Italiam tenuit
sentences.l: and with moderate west winds across the Ionian sea, at the rising of the sixth daughter of Pallas, he reached Italy
sentences.i: and with light west winds across the Ionian sea he made Italy at the rising of the sixth dawn
sentences.n: “Sextae Pallantidos ortu” is a small riddle: Pallantis is Aurora, the Dawn, called the daughter of the Titan Pallas, and “Pallantidos” is a Greek genitive singular in -idos, kept unlatinized. The sixth rising of Dawn is the sixth day out — Latin verse counts a voyage in dawns. “Zephyri” are properly the west winds, though Latin verse uses the name freely of any mild breeze — which is as well, since the course here runs westward. “Tenuit” used of a ship means to hold course for and reach a landfall.

sentences.t:
praeterque Lacinia templo
nobilitata deae Scylaceaque litora fertur;
sentences.l: and he is carried past the Lacinian heights, made famous by the goddess's temple, and the Scylacean shores;
sentences.i: and is borne past the Lacinian headland, famous for the goddess's temple, and the shores of Scylaceum;
sentences.n: The Lacinian promontory, in Bruttium at the toe of Italy, carried the temple of Juno Lacinia, one of the great sanctuaries of the south; “deae” is that goddess, named only as “the goddess” because everyone knew which. From here to 718 the poem turns into a coasting itinerary: place after place named in the order a ship going north would pass them. “Fertur” is passive, “is carried”, of a hull moving with wind and current rather than being rowed.

sentences.t:
linquit Iapygiam laevisque Amphrisia remis
saxa fugit, dextra praerupta Celennia parte,
sentences.l: he leaves Iapygia, and with oars on the left flees the Amphrisian rocks, on the right side the sheer Celennian crags,
sentences.i: he leaves Iapygia behind, runs past the Amphrisian rocks with his oars to port, and the sheer Celennian crags to starboard,
sentences.n: “Laevis … remis” and “dextra … parte” give the bearings from on board, left and right of the ship rather than points of the compass — this is how a sailing direction was described. “Fugit” is transitive here: to flee a thing is to run past and clear of it. Magnus prints “Celennia”; some editions print “Cocinthia”, the Cocinthian cape, which is a different point on the same coast — the reading is genuinely uncertain.

sentences.t:
Romethiumque legit Caulonaque Naryciamque,
evincitque fretum Siculique angusta Pelori
Hippotadaeque domos regis Temesesque metalla,
sentences.l: and he coasts Romethium and Caulon and Narycia, and wins through the strait and the narrows of Sicilian Pelorus and the houses of the king, Hippotes' son and the mines of Temese,
sentences.i: coasts Romethium, Caulon and Narycia, forces the strait and the narrows of Sicilian Pelorus, the halls of the king born of Hippotes, and the mines of Temese,
sentences.n: “Legere” of a ship is to “gather” a coast — to run close in along it, picking the shore up piece by piece; there is no single English verb for it. “Evincit” is “wins right through”, the word for forcing a hard passage, and the passage here is the strait of Messina, with Pelorus the north-eastern cape of Sicily standing over it. “Hippotadae regis” is the son of Hippotes, Aeolus, king of the winds, whose islands lie north of Sicily. Temese in Bruttium was famous for its copper.

sentences.t: Leucosiamque petit tepidique rosaria Paesti.
sentences.l: and he makes for Leucosia and the rose-gardens of warm Paestum.
sentences.n: The roses of Paestum were proverbial for flowering twice in a year, and the town is named by them rather than by anything else. “Tepidus” of a place means mild, warm-tempered in climate. Leucosia is the little island off the Lucanian coast just south of Paestum, named after one of the Sirens; Parthenope, another of them, comes at 712.

sentences.t:
Inde legit Capreas promunturiumque Minervae
et Surrentino generosos palmite colles
sentences.l: From there he coasts Capreae and the promontory of Minerva and the hills noble with the Surrentine vine-shoot
sentences.i: From there he skirts Capreae, Minerva's headland, and the hills made noble by the vines of Surrentum
sentences.n: The “promunturium Minervae” is the cape at the tip of the Sorrentine peninsula, with its shrine of Minerva. “Generosus” is properly “of good stock, well born”, the word used of a fine breed of horse or a good vine-stock, so calling hills “generosos … palmite” gives the vine's pedigree to the ground it grows on. “Palmes” is the vine-shoot itself; Surrentine wine was among the best in Italy.

sentences.t:
Herculeamque urbem Stabiasque et in otia natam
Parthenopen et ab hac Cumaeae templa Sibyllae.
sentences.l: and the Herculean city and Stabiae and Parthenope born for leisure, and after her the temples of the Cumaean Sibyl.
sentences.i: and the city of Hercules, and Stabiae, and Parthenope born for idleness, and past her the temple of the Cumaean Sibyl.
sentences.n: The “Herculean city” is Herculaneum, named from its founder-hero. Parthenope is the old Greek name of Naples, after the Siren said to be buried there — and “in otia natam”, born for leisure, is a judgement on the city's character delivered in three words. The Sibyl's shrine at Cumae closes the stretch of coast around the bay; Liternum, the Volturnus and Sinuessa, all of them still Campanian, follow before Latium begins.

sentences.t:
Hinc calidi fontes lentisciferumque tenetur
Liternum multamque trahens sub gurgite harenam
Volturnus niveisque frequens Sinuessa columbis
sentences.l: From here the warm springs are made for, and mastic-bearing Liternum, and Volturnus dragging much sand beneath his flood, and Sinuessa thronged with snow-white doves,
sentences.i: From here the hot springs are made for, and mastic-bearing Liternum, and Volturnus dragging its load of sand under the current, and Sinuessa crowded with snow-white doves,
sentences.n: “Tenetur” is passive and singular, and the grammar is worth pausing on: the long list of places from here to “Antium” at 718 is its subject, and the verb agrees only with the nearest of them, the neuter singular “Liternum”. Turning the sentence passive puts the coast in the nominative and the ship out of sight altogether — the land is what is reached, not the traveller who reaches it. “Lentisciferum”, mastic-bearing, is one of the long compound adjectives Ovid coins for catalogues like this. The Volturnus was known for the silt it carried.

sentences.t:
Minturnaeque graves et quam tumulavit alumnus
Antiphataeque domus Trachasque obsessa palude
et tellus Circaea et spissi litoris Antium.
sentences.l: and heavy Minturnae, and she whom her nursling buried, and the house of Antiphates, and Trachas beset by marsh, and the Circaean land, and Antium of the packed shore.
sentences.i: and oppressive Minturnae, and she whom her foster-son buried, and the house of Antiphates, and Trachas hemmed in by its marsh, and the land of Circe, and Antium of the close-packed shore.
sentences.n: “Gravis” of a place means unhealthy, heavy on those who live there; the marshes around Minturnae were notorious. “Quam tumulavit alumnus” names a person instead of a place and leaves you to work it out: Caieta, the nurse buried by her foster-son Aeneas, whose name the harbour keeps. “Antiphatae domus” is Formiae, where legend put the Laestrygonian king Antiphates. “Trachas” is Tarracina, and “tellus Circaea” the Circeian promontory, Circe's headland.

sentences.t:
Huc ubi veliferam nautae advertere carinam
(asper enim iam pontus erat),
sentences.l: When the sailors had turned the sail-bearing keel in to this place (for by now the sea was rough),
sentences.i: When the sailors had brought the sail-carrying ship in here — for by now the sea was running rough —
sentences.n: “Advertere” is “adverterunt”, the -ēre perfect once more, and “advertere carinam” is the technical phrase for putting a ship's head in to shore. “Veliferam”, sail-bearing, is another coined compound, and “carinam” is the keel for the whole ship, as at 644 and 694. The parenthesis supplies the reason for putting in at all: they are running for shelter, not calling by choice — which is why the god's visit to his father's temple is a chance one.

sentences.t:
deus explicat orbes
perque sinus crebros et magna volumina labens
templa parentis init flavum tangentia litus.
sentences.l: the god unfolds his coils and, gliding through crowded curves and great windings, enters his father's temple, which touches the yellow shore.
sentences.i: the god unwound his coils and, gliding in close curve after curve and long rolling folds, entered his father's temple, which touches the tawny shore.
sentences.n: “Explicat orbes” is literally “unfolds his circles”: a snake has to unroll itself to move at all, and the verb is exact rather than decorative. “Sinus crebros et magna volumina” distinguishes two kinds of movement — the short tight bends and the long sweeping rolls of a snake's track. “Parentis” is Apollo, whose temple stood at Antium. “Flavus”, tawny-yellow, is the standing colour word for sand and for silted water.

sentences.t:
Aequore placato patrias Epidaurius aras
linquit et hospitio iuncti sibi numinis usus
sentences.l: With the sea calmed, the Epidaurian leaves his father's altars and, having used the hospitality of the divinity joined to him,
sentences.i: The sea calmed, the god of Epidaurus left his father's altars and, having taken the hospitality of the god who was kin to him,
sentences.n: “Aequore placato”, another ablative absolute. “Epidaurius” names the god from the city of his cult, which is exactly how a Roman would have referred to him — and it is one more of the periphrases that stand in for the name this part never uses. “Usus” governs the ablative: “utor” is one of the small group of deponent verbs that take the ablative rather than the accusative. “Hospitium” is not vague warmth but a formal Roman institution, the standing tie between host and guest — and here the tie is kinship, since the host is his father.

sentences.t:
litoream tractu squamae crepitantis harenam
sulcat et innixus moderamine navis in alta
puppe caput posuit,
sentences.l: he furrows the shore sand with the dragging of his rattling scale, and, propped on the ship's steering-oar, laid his head on the high stern,
sentences.i: he furrowed the sand of the beach with the drag of his rasping scales, and, propped on the ship's steering-oar, laid his head on the high stern,
sentences.n: “Sulcat” is to plough a furrow, and the track a heavy snake leaves in sand is exactly that. “Tractu squamae crepitantis” uses the singular “squama” for the whole skin, and “crepitare” is the dry rattling sound of scales dragged over sand — the line is heard as much as seen. “Moderamen” is the steering-oar, from “moderor”, to govern: the thing by which a ship is controlled. Note the present “sulcat” and the perfect “posuit” inside one sentence, the tense alternation again.

sentences.t:
donec Castrumque sacrasque
Lavini sedes Tiberinaque ad ostia venit.
sentences.l: until he came to Castrum and the sacred seats of Lavinium and the mouths of the Tiber.
sentences.i: until he came to Castrum, and the holy settlement of Lavinium, and the mouths of the Tiber.
sentences.n: “Donec” with the perfect indicative marks the point actually reached, not a mere intention. “Castrum” is Castrum Inui on the Latian coast; “Lavini sedes” is Lavinium, the town Aeneas founded when he landed — so the coasting list, which began among Greek colonies, ends on the Trojan foundations of Latium, and the very next thing named will be Vesta's fire brought from Troy. “Ostia” is plural because the Tiber reaches the sea by more than one mouth.

sentences.t:
Huc omnis populi passim matrumque patrumque
obvia turba ruit,
sentences.l: Here the whole crowd of the people, from everywhere, of mothers and of fathers, rushes to meet him,
sentences.i: Here the whole people rushed out from every side to meet him, mothers and fathers together,
sentences.n: “Obvia” is an adjective doing the work of an English verb: “in the way, meeting”, so “obvia turba ruit” is a crowd that rushes in the act of meeting him. “Matrumque patrumque”, the doubled “-que” binding the pair, is a standard way of saying the entire population, women and men — not two separate groups but one body named by both halves. “Passim” is scattered, from all directions at once.

sentences.t:
quaeque ignes, Troica, servant,
Vesta, tuos, laetoque deum clamore salutant.
sentences.l: and those women who guard your fires, Trojan Vesta, and they greet the god with joyful shouting.
sentences.i: and the women who keep your fires, Trojan Vesta; and they greet the god with a shout of joy.
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside in mid-sentence to address the goddess — “Troica … Vesta … tuos” — the same apostrophe he used to the Roman at 654, and the vocative and its epithet are torn apart: “Troica” is lodged inside the relative clause at 730 and “Vesta” left to open 731, with “tuos” held back to that line too, away from its “ignes”. The women “who guard your fires” are the Vestal Virgins, named by what they do rather than by their title. “Troica” because Vesta's fire was held to have come from Troy with Aeneas — which is why Lavinium was named two lines earlier.

sentences.t:
Quaque per adversas navis cita ducitur undas,
tura super ripas aris ex ordine factis
parte ab utraque sonant et odorant aera fumis,
sentences.l: And wherever the swift ship is drawn through the opposing waves, incense sounds on both sides above the banks, on altars built in a row, and scents the air with its smoke,
sentences.i: And wherever the swift ship was hauled up against the current, incense crackled above the banks on either side, on altars set out in a line, and perfumed the air with its smoke,
sentences.n: “Quaque” is the local relative adverb, “and by whatever way”, hence “wherever” — not a form of “qui”. “Adversas … undas” is the standard phrase for a current a boat has to fight, and “ducitur” is passive because the ship is being towed upstream from the bank, not sailed. “Sonant” of incense is the crackle and spit of the grains as they hit the fire; the altars are heard before the smoke is smelt.

sentences.t: ictaque coniectos incalfacit hostia cultros.
sentences.l: and the struck victim warms the knives driven into it.
sentences.i: and the stricken victim warmed the knives buried in it.
sentences.n: The line reverses the picture you expect: not the knife that hurts the beast but the beast that warms the knife, because the blood is what carries the heat. “Hostia” is the sacrificial animal, “cultri” the sacrificial knives. The two perfect passive participles, “icta” and “coniectos”, stand side by side at the head of the line, so both wounds — the animal's and the knife's burial in it — arrive before the verb does.

sentences.t: Iamque caput rerum, Romanam intraverat urbem:
sentences.l: And now he had entered the head of the world, the Roman city:
sentences.i: And now he had entered the head of the world, the city of Rome:
sentences.n: “Caput rerum”, literally “the head of things”, is the standing Roman phrase for Rome as the capital of the world, and it stands in apposition to “Romanam … urbem”, which is why the edition sets a comma between them. “Intraverat” has no expressed subject: the word “serpens” does not arrive until the next line, so the sentence gives Rome its grandest title before it says what has just come into it.

sentences.t:
erigitur serpens summoque acclinia malo
colla movet sedesque sibi circumspicit aptas.
sentences.l: the serpent raises himself and moves his neck, leaning against the top of the mast, and looks about for a seat fitting for himself.
sentences.i: the serpent reared, moved his neck where it leaned on the masthead, and looked about him for a fitting place to settle.
sentences.n: “Erigitur” is passive in form but middle in sense — “he raises himself” — the same usage as “Vertar” at 661. “Summo … malo” is “on the top of the mast”: “summus” with a noun means the top part of the thing, not the highest of several. The neuter plural “colla” is used of one neck, as “pectoribus” was of one chest at 673. And “sedes … aptas” answers the prayer at 667–668, that the god himself would show where he wanted to settle: he is now doing it, by looking.

sentences.t:
Scinditur in geminas partes circumfluus amnis
(Insula nomen habet), laterumque a parte duorum
porrigit aequales media tellure lacertos.
sentences.l: The river that flows round is split into twin parts (the Island is its name), and from the region of its two sides it stretches out equal arms with the land in the middle.
sentences.i: The river divides in two and flows around (the place is called the Island), and from either side it stretches out equal arms with the land between them.
sentences.n: This is the aetiology the invocation promised at 622–625, and the language answers it exactly: “circumfluus amnis” here against “circumflua … insula” there, and the name “Insula” given outright. The Tiber Island, where the temple of Aesculapius stood from 291 BC, is the point the whole voyage has been travelling towards. “Lacertos” is the upper arm of a human body, so the river is given a body and the island lies in its embrace. “Geminus” is properly “twin”, born of one birth — the two channels are a pair, not merely two.

sentences.t:
Huc se de Latia pinu Phoebeius anguis
contulit et finem, specie caeleste resumpta,
luctibus imposuit venitque salutifer urbi.
sentences.l: Here the Phoebean serpent betook himself from the Latian pine, and, with his heavenly form taken up again, put an end to the mourning, and came bringing health to the city.
sentences.i: Here the serpent of Phoebus took himself from the Latin pine and, resuming his heavenly form, put an end to the mourning, and came as a bringer of health to the city.
sentences.n: “Se contulit” — the reflexive with “confero” is the ordinary Latin for betaking oneself somewhere. “De Latia pinu”: the pine stands for the ship built out of it, the same part-for-whole as “carina” for the hull earlier. “Specie caeleste resumpta” is a last ablative absolute, and it undoes the change the god announced at 661–662. Note the form “caeleste”: it is the ablative singular of “caelestis” in -e rather than the more usual -i, an alternative that verse allows. And “salutifer” closes the episode on the very word the prayer at Delphi opened with (“salutifera … sorte”, 632) — the health asked for is the health delivered.
